title: How a Sacred Leaf Became a $100 Billion Empire
fullText: In 1989, 5 minutes after takeoff from Bogota, Colombia, a bomb tore Avianca Flight 203 apart in midair, killing all 107 people on board. It was not an act of war. It was a business decision ordered by one man who believed an enemy of his might be on that plane. He was not. That same year, that same man was reportedly earning so much cash that his organization spent $2,500 every month on rubber bands just to keep the bills bundled. Forbes magazine had already named him one of the richest men on the planet. With a fortune estimated as high as $30 billion. His home city of Medellin was on its way to becoming the murder capital of the world. And his country was burying [music] judges, journalists, police officers, and three separate presidential candidates. And at the center of all of it, the thing all that blood and money revolved around was not gold, not oil, not weapons, [music] a leaf. A small green leaf from a mountain shrub so mild that chewing it delivers [music] less of a jolt than a strong cup of coffee. A leaf that Andean farmers have grown for roughly 8,000 years. A leaf that was once [music] an ingredient in the most famous soft drink on earth. So, how did a humble Andean shrub become the engine of the most profitable criminal industry in human history? How did it charm popes and presidents, revolutionize modern surgery, and rewrite the drug laws of nearly every nation on the planet? That was 1989. But the story of coca begins about 8,000 years earlier. In the dry foothills of the Andes, in what is now northern Peru. In the Nanchoc Valley of Peru, archaeologists excavating the floors of houses abandoned roughly 8,000 years ago found two things buried together. Coca leaves and pieces of calcium-rich rock that had been burned and scraped. That pairing matters because it is exactly how coca is still consumed across the Andes today. A chewer tucks a wad of leaves into the cheek along with a pinch of alkaline ash or lime. And the alkaline material coaxes the active compounds out of the leaf. Which means the people of the Nanchoc Valley were not simply nibbling on an interesting plant. 8,000 years ago, they had already worked out the chemistry required [music] to unlock it. They did not know the word alkaloid. They were doing it anyway. And it is worth being clear about what coca actually does because it is almost nothing like the white powder it would eventually become. Chewed leaf releases its compounds slowly and gently. It dulls hunger. It blunts fatigue. It takes the edge off cold and altitude sickness. The leaves themselves carry calcium, >> [music] >> iron, and vitamins. Now, picture where these people lived. A vertical world of thin air and thinner harvests, where farmers [music] work terraced fields at 10, 12, 14,000 ft above sea level. In that world, coca was not a vice. It was survival equipment. It was the difference between finishing the harvest and collapsing halfway through it. Over centuries, Andean farmers domesticated the wild shrub. Selecting and replanting until they had created a hardy plant that thrives on steep, misty mountainsides, >> [music] >> where almost nothing else of value will grow. The name itself likely comes from an Aymara word meaning simply the tree, not a tree, the tree. That tells you everything about its status. By about 2,000 years ago, coca was woven into every civilization along the Andes. Moche and Nazca potters sculpted figures with one cheek distinctively bulging, the unmistakable portrait of a coca chewer. And those ceramics survive by the thousands. But, it was the Inca who elevated the leaf into something close to a state religion. At its height in the 15th century, the Inca empire stretched roughly 2,500 miles down the spine of South America. Governing perhaps 10 million people. And coca sat near the center of its spiritual and political machinery. Priests [music] read the fall of coca leaves to divine the future. The leaf was offered to Pachamama, the Earth Mother, before planting, before building, before [music] burying the dead. A practice that continues in the Andes to [music] this day. According to Inca legend, coca was a gift from the sun god. Delivered through a beautiful woman called Mama Coca. Now, that story is almost certainly a myth. But, the fact that the Inca wrote the leaf into their theology tells you how much it mattered. It mattered in practical terms, too. The empire ran on a relay system of runners called chasqui. Who sprinted between roadside stations carrying messages from the coast to the capital at Cusco. The system could reportedly move a message around 150 miles in a single day. A pony express running at full gallop four centuries early at 12,000 ft on leaves. And there is one more detail. And it is a haunting one. High on the summit of the Llullaillaco volcano at over 22,000 ft. Archaeologists found the frozen bodies of three Inca children left as ritual sacrifices 500 years ago. Chemical analysis of their hair showed heavy coca use in their final months. The leaf eased them up a mountain they would never come down from. Sacred does not always mean gentle. Then in 1532 168 Spaniards under Francisco Pizarro ambushed the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca and the greatest empire in the Americas began to collapse. The Spanish took the gold, they took the silver. The leaf at first they despised. [music] Catholic clergy saw coca everywhere in native ritual and concluded it was an instrument of idolatry. The first council of Lima in 1552 condemned it. And one churchman reportedly dismissed the leaf as a talisman of the devil. And then in 1545 the Spanish found a mountain and [music] every theological objection in the empire suddenly became negotiable. The mountain was Cerro Rico at Potosi [music] in modern Bolivia over 13,000 feet above sea level. It turned out to be the richest silver strike ever discovered and by some estimates it would eventually supply more than half of all the silver flowing through the early modern world. To dig it out the Spanish revived and perverted an old Inca labor draft called the mita forcing tens of [music] thousands of Andean men into the mines. Conditions were medieval. Miners descended on rope ladders into candlelit tunnels and stayed underground for up to a week at a time >> [music] >> breathing rock dust in the dark, hauling ore on their backs up hundreds of feet of ladders. Outside at the refineries, workers waded through the toxic mercury [music] used to separate the silver, and the poisoning showed in their trembling hands and falling hair. The air at that altitude is thin and freezing. Food was scarce, and the Spanish noticed something. Men with coca worked longer, ate less, [music] and complained less. The leaf the church had wanted to burn was, it turned out, extraordinarily good for productivity. The moral debate ended almost overnight. The Spanish crown declared coca essential to the well-being of the native workers. Colonial planters took over the coca fields of the warm valleys, and a massive supply chain >> [music] >> began hauling leaf up to the mines. By the late 1500s, coca was one of the most traded commodities in Peru. And the church, the same institution that had called the leaf demonic, was collecting a tithe on every basket. Bishops were, in a very real sense, partly funded by coca. [music] Here is the part that should make you angry. Potosi silver was minted into pieces [music] of eight that became the first truly global currency. Coins that bought spices in Manila, silk in China, and armies across Europe. Popular accounts claim that millions died in the mines over the colonial centuries. Historians still debate the true number. What no one disputes is that generations of Andean [music] men were marched into that mountain, and that coca is what kept them digging. Coca did not just witness the plunder of the Andes. Coca subsidized it. Behind every piece of eight, there was a leaf. And yet, for the next 300 years, >> [music] >> Europe itself barely touched the stuff. Here is why. Coca [music] leaves lose their potency within weeks, and the voyage from Peru took months. The samples that reached Europe arrived stale, brown, and unimpressive, and European doctors mostly [music] shrugged. The Atlantic Ocean was, in effect, the cage that held coca. Then, in a German laboratory, the cage [music] broke open. In 1860, a 25-year-old chemistry student in Göttingen named Albert Niemann isolated the active compound of the leaf in pure crystalline form. He named it cocaine, and he noted, almost in passing, that it numbed the tongue. Niemann died the following year, and in one of history's darker footnotes, his other research project involved the sulfur compound that would later become mustard gas. But his white crystals survived him, and they were about to conquer the Western world. The first man to get rich on coca was not a doctor. He was a marketer. In 1863, a Corsican chemist named Angelo Mariani began steeping coca leaves in Bordeaux wine and selling the result as Vin Mariani, a tonic for energy, health, and vitality. Think of it as the Red Bull of the 19th [music] century, if Red Bull came in a Bordeaux bottle and carried an endorsement from the Vatican. Because it did. Pope Leo the 13th was reportedly so fond of Vin Mariani that he awarded Mariani a Vatican gold medal and allowed his face to appear on the advertising posters. His successor, Pius the 10th, drank it, too. Thomas Edison endorsed it. Queen Victoria was said to enjoy it. And Ulysses S. Grant, dying [music] of throat cancer and racing to finish his memoirs to save his family from bankruptcy, took it as he wrote. Two popes, an inventor, a queen, and a president. Mariani had assembled the greatest celebrity endorsement roster of his century for a product whose key ingredient would one day carry a mandatory prison sentence. Medicine came running right behind the marketers. In 1884, a young, ambitious, and chronically broke Viennese neurologist named [music] Sigmund Freud published a paper titled Uber Coca, an almost giddy hymn of praise. He recommended cocaine for fatigue, for depression, for digestive trouble, and, most fatefully, as a cure for morphine addiction. He tested that last idea on his close friend, Ernst von Fleischl-Marxow, a brilliant physiologist hooked on morphine after a botched amputation left him in constant pain. At first, it seemed to work. Then, Fleischl began taking enormous quantities of cocaine, developed [music] full-blown psychosis, spent nights convinced that insects were crawling beneath his skin, and died in 1891 at the age of 45, addicted to both drugs at [music] once. Freud spent years trying to live the episode down. But that same year, 1884, [music] another young Viennese doctor read about cocaine and saw something completely different. [music] His name was Carl Koller, and he was an eye specialist with a brutal problem. Ether anesthesia, the miracle of the age, was nearly useless for eye surgery because patients coughed and retched [music] as they came around, ruining delicate incisions. Eye operations were therefore often performed on conscious patients [music] held still, watching the blade approach. Koller remembered that cocaine numbed the tongue, dissolved a small amount in water, and dripped it into an eye. The eye [music] went completely numb. In September of 1884, his findings were presented to a medical congress in Heidelberg and surgery changed overnight. [music] For the first time in human history, a doctor could switch off pain in one precise part of the body while the patient sat calmly awake. And this is the part that does not get enough credit. >> [music] >> Every local anesthetic that followed, Novocain in 1905, lidocaine in the 1940s, the injection that numbs your jaw at the dentist [music] today, every single one is a chemical descendant of cocaine, redesigned to keep the numbness and lose the rest. The next time a dentist tells you that you will feel a little pinch, you are living inside Carl Koller's discovery. Medicine, however, learned the dark side of the drug quickly [music] and personally. William Halsted, the New York surgeon who used cocaine to invent the nerve block, experimented on himself and [music] his students so enthusiastically that he became severely addicted. His friends smuggled him onto a boat, then into an asylum where doctors treated his cocaine habit with morphine, simply trading one dependency [music] for another. Halsted went on to become a founding professor at Johns Hopkins, a pioneer of modern surgery, and the man who introduced rubber surgical gloves, and he remained quietly dependent for the rest of his celebrated life. One of the fathers of American surgery was a functioning addict for decades, [music] and his colleagues guarded the secret like a state treasure. Meanwhile, in Atlanta, Georgia, a wounded Confederate veteran was about to make Coca immortal. John Pemberton was a pharmacist who had been slashed across the chest by a saber in the final weeks of the Civil War, and like thousands of injured veterans had come home addicted [music] to morphine. Searching for a cure, and for a paycheck, he cooked up his own imitation of Vin Mariani. Then, in 1886, [music] his county went dry, and Pemberton scrambled to create a non-alcoholic version, a sweet syrup of coca leaf extract and caffeine-rich cola nut mixed with carbonated water and sold at a pharmacy soda fountain for 5 cents a glass. His bookkeeper, Frank Robinson, suggested a name and sketched it in flowing script, Coca-Cola. It was marketed not as a treat, but as medicine, a brain tonic for headaches and nervous exhaustion. Pemberton, sick and still addicted, sold off his rights for a total of around $2,300, roughly $70,000 in today's money, and died in 1888, 2 years before his invention began its march across the planet. He never saw a dime of the empire. And Coca-Cola was only the famous tip of a very large iceberg, because in the 1880s and 90s, cocaine was simply everywhere in American life. Pharmacies sold cocaine toothache drops, marketed openly for children at 15 cents [music] a box. There were cocaine catarrh powders, cocaine hay fever remedies, cocaine cigarettes, cocaine wines. [music] For a time, the Sears Roebuck catalog offered a cocaine kit, syringe included, for about a dollar fifty. This was not a black market. There was no black market. Cocaine was as legal as flour and considerably better advertised. The crash came fast. By the turn of the century, doctors were filling journals with reports of ruined patients, and the national romance with the miracle drug curdled into fear. Coca-Cola quietly removed the active cocaine from its formula by about 1903, switching to spent leaves with the drug already extracted. But the backlash, when it fully arrived, was not driven mainly by medicine. It was driven by racism. And this part of the story has to be told plainly. In the early 1900s, southern newspapers and even medical journals began publishing lurid, fabricated stories about cocaine-crazed black men, claiming the drug gave them superhuman strength, >> [music] >> made them immune to bullets, and drove them to violence. In 1914, the New York Times ran a physician's article describing so-called cocaine fiends as a new southern menace. Some southern police departments reportedly switched to larger-caliber revolvers, citing the myth. None of it was true, all of it worked. The 1906 Pure Food and Drug Act forced manufacturers to disclose cocaine on their labels. The 1914 Harrison Narcotic Act [music] taxed and restricted the drug into effective prohibition. And by 1922, [music] imports were essentially banned. Other nations followed, international treaties locked the door. And by the middle of the 20th century, cocaine had all but vanished from American life. Its role as the everyman's stimulant filled, with no apparent irony, by perfectly legal amphetamine pills. But, cocaine was not gone. It was waiting. If you are finding this interesting, hit subscribe. We cover stories like this every week, and you will not want to miss what comes next. [music] Because what came next was the 1970s, and the second act of cocaine made its first [music] look quaint. As amphetamines were finally restricted and disco lit up, cocaine returned as the glamour drug of the decade, expensive, imported, and gleaming with status. At Studio 54, it was practically part of the decor. On Wall Street, it was practically part of the work day. At roughly $100 a gram, several hundred dollars in today's money, it was marketed by its sheer price as the champagne of drugs, [music] and mainstream magazines ran cover stories treating it as a fashionable, relatively harmless indulgence. American demand exploded. And 2,000 miles to the south, a handful of men in Medellin, Colombia, realized they were sitting on the trade opportunity of the century. Colombia did not even grow much coca at the time, but it sat directly between the leaf fields of Peru and Bolivia, and the wealthiest consumer market on earth, with two coastlines, endless jungle airstrips, and a long tradition of smuggling. Pablo Escobar and his partners [music] industrialized the route. Product was refined in makeshift jungle laboratories and flown north in small planes, hundreds of kilograms at a time. [music] One partner, Carlos Lehder, simply bought most of a Bohemian island called Norman's Cay and turned it into a private refueling base 200 miles off the Florida coast. At its peak, the Medellín Cartel supplied an estimated 80% of the cocaine entering the United States with revenues that some estimates put as high as $60 million a day. The money became a physical problem. The brother of Escobar, who kept the books, later claimed the organization spent that $2,500 a month on rubber bands >> [music] >> and wrote off roughly 10% of its cash every year because rats ate it or mold ruined it in storage. Think about that for a second. Their accounting included a line item for rats. Escobar built a sprawling estate with its own private zoo stocked with elephants, giraffes, and four hippopotamuses. Remember the hippos, they will matter later. Then came the war, and here the story turns fully dark. The policy of Escobar toward officials was plata o plomo, silver or lead. Take the bribe or take the bullet. When the justice minister [music] of Colombia, Rodrigo Lara Bonilla, moved against the cartel, he was machine-gunned in his car in 1984. When the government threatened extradition to the United States, the one punishment Escobar truly feared, he answered with a campaign of terror without precedent in the hemisphere. Judges were murdered by the dozen. Journalists were murdered. Police officers were murdered for a bounty, [music] hundreds of them in Medellín alone. In August of 1989, the leading presidential candidate, Luis Carlos Galán, >> [music] >> was assassinated at a campaign rally, and two more presidential candidates were killed within the year. In November, cartel bombers destroyed Avianca Flight 203, the plane from the beginning of this story, killing 107 people in an attempt to murder one politician who was not even on board. By 1991, Medellín was recording roughly 380 homicides per 100,000 residents, the highest urban murder rate on Earth. Escobar eventually negotiated his own imprisonment [music] in a luxury prison he designed himself, complete with a soccer pitch and a bar, then escaped when the government tried to move him. 16 months later, on December 2nd, >> [music] >> 1993, he was shot dead on a Medellín rooftop, one day after his 44th birthday. And here is the uncomfortable truth about that famous rooftop. The cocaine trade did not miss a single shipment. The Cali Cartel absorbed the market, then shattered into smaller groups when its own leaders fell, and control of the routes migrated north to Mexican organizations, which [music] transformed from couriers into owners. The consequences are still unfolding. Since the Mexican government declared war on the cartels in 2006, the country has suffered well over [music] 300,000 homicides and more than 100,000 disappearances, a toll entangled with, though not solely caused by, the northbound flow of drugs, cocaine chief among them. Kill the kingpin, and the market simply promotes someone new. Columbia proved it. Mexico is still proving it. And while Columbia bled, the drug itself was mutating in American cities. In the early and mid-1980s, dealers began selling cocaine in a cheap, smokable form known as crack in single doses that cost as little as $5. A drug that had been a status symbol for the rich was suddenly available on the poorest blocks in America, delivering a high that was faster, harsher, shorter, and far more compulsive. The results were catastrophic. Spiraling addiction, open-air drug markets, and turf wars that drove homicide rates in some cities [music] to record levels. In June of 1986, [music] college basketball star Len Bias, 2 days after being drafted by the Boston Celtics, died of cocaine-induced heart failure, and his death >> [music] >> detonated a national panic. It hardly mattered that the evidence pointed to powder cocaine rather than crack. Within months, Congress passed the Anti-Drug Abuse Act of 1986, [music] which set a now infamous threshold. Possessing 5 g of crack triggered the same 5-year mandatory minimum sentence as 500 g of powder. The same drug in two different forms punished at a ratio of 100 to 1, 100 to 1. And because crack was concentrated in poor black neighborhoods while powder circulated in wealthier white ones, the sentencing gap fell almost entirely along racial [music] lines. By the 1990s, the overwhelming majority of federal crack defendants were black, even though national surveys suggested most users of the drug were not. Some of the loudest horror stories of the era, like the prophesied generation of permanently damaged so-called crack babies, were later found by researchers to have been badly exaggerated. The prison sentences were not exaggerated. They were served. In 2010, Congress reduced the ratio from 100 to 1 down to 18 to 1. Reduced [music] not eliminated. So, follow the money because tens of billions of dollars a year do not fit under a mattress. They go into banks. In 2010, Wachovia, then one of the largest banks in the United States, admitted it had failed to monitor around 378 billion dollars in transfers from Mexican currency exchange houses that the cartels use freely. The penalty came to about 160 million dollars. Less than 2% of the profits of the bank for a single year. And not one banker went to prison. Two years later, HSBC paid 1.9 billion dollars over similar failures. And investigators described cartel cash arriving in boxes built to fit [music] the exact dimensions of the teller windows. It was the tobacco playbook applied to [music] finance. Deny, delay, settle quietly, and carry on. Even governments have not escaped the gravity of this money. In 1996, a newspaper series alleged that traffickers linked to CIA-backed rebels in Nicaragua had helped feed the early crack trade. Later, official investigations [music] rejected the strongest versions of that claim, but the Inspector General of the CIA acknowledged that the agency had worked with suppliers accused of trafficking and [music] had been slow to cut them loose. The full truth remains contested. The pattern does not, which brings us to now and to a set of numbers that should end [music] any illusion that this war has been won. Since 1971, the United States alone has spent an estimated 1 trillion dollars fighting the war on drugs. The result, according to the United Nations [music] is that global coca cultivation recently hit the highest level ever recorded. Roughly [music] 350,000 hectares, with well over 200,000 in Colombia alone. Enough to yield an estimated 2,700 tons of cocaine in a single year. Roughly 23 million people worldwide use the drug in the past year. Feeding a trade worth well over 100 billion dollars annually by most estimates. And the fastest growth is no longer in the United States at all, but in Europe, where the port of Antwerp seized roughly 116 tons in a single recent year. And wastewater testing shows consumption climbing across the continent. The trade now carries new dangers, from batches contaminated with the far deadlier synthetic opioid fentanyl, to what researchers call narco-deforestation, as trafficking money bulldozes rainforests across the Amazon and Central America to launder itself through cattle ranches and airstrips. But cocaine is far more than a crime statistic. And this next part tends to catch people off guard. Cocaine is still a legal medicine in the United States. It sits in schedule two, rather than schedule one, precisely because it has accepted medical uses. [music] And as recently as 2017 and 2020, the FDA approved new prescription cocaine solutions for use in surgery. Ear, nose, and throat surgeons still reach for it because it does something no modern substitute does quite as well. It numbs tissue and shrinks blood vessels at the same time. Right now, in American operating rooms, pharmaceutical cocaine is being [music] used lawfully on patients. And the supply chain behind that fact is even stranger. In Maywood, New Jersey, a chemical firm called the Stepan Company holds a rare federal registration to legally import coca leaves by the ton. The medicinal extract goes to a pharmaceutical manufacturer. The leftover leaf flavoring, with the drug removed, goes to exactly one famous customer. The Coca-Cola Company. There is, in other words, still coca in Coca-Cola, imported and processed under federal license, more than a century after the cocaine came out. Meanwhile, a 2009 study found cocaine residue on roughly nine out of every 10 United States banknotes. [music] Which means the odds are good that a microscopic trace of this entire story is folded in your wallet right now. And the hippos, the four that Escobar imported, >> [music] >> escaped after his death, thrived in the rivers of Colombia, and have multiplied into a feral population estimated [music] at well over 150 animals. The largest wild hippo herd outside Africa, now officially declared an invasive species, and the subject of a government sterilization campaign. His cocaine empire collapsed in a day. His hippos are still winning. There is one more place this story has to visit, and that is back where it began. In Bolivia and Peru, the coca leaf itself remains legal, sold by the sack in public markets, brewed into a tea that hotels in La Paz and Cusco hand to altitude-sick tourists at check-in. In 2006, Bolivia elected Evo Morales, a former leader of the coca growers unions, as [music] president, and his government wrote the leaf into the constitution as cultural heritage under a simple slogan, "Coca, yes. Cocaine, no." Bolivia even briefly withdrew from the United Nations Drug Convention and rejoined with a formal reservation protecting traditional [music] coca chewing. And in 2023, Bolivia formally asked the World Health Organization to re-examine how the coca leaf is classified >> [music] >> under international law, a scientific review that as of this year is still underway. More than 60 years after the leaf was listed alongside heroin, the world is finally re-asking an 8,000-year-old question. Is the plant the problem, or is it what we did to the plant? It was there when the first farmers of the Ñanchoc Valley pressed leaves and burned lime into their house floors 8,000 years ago. It was there in the cheeks of the runners who carried the messages of an empire along the spine of the Andes. It was there in the freezing tunnels of Potosí, keeping conscripted men digging for the silver that built the modern world. It was there in the wine of two popes, in the letters of Freud, in the eyedropper that switched off pain and changed surgery forever. It was there behind the marble counter of an Atlanta pharmacy, 5 cents a glass. It was there at Studio 54, in the cargo holds over the Caribbean, in the courtrooms of the 1980s, and in the ledgers of banks too big to jail. >> [music] >> And it is still here. It is in the numbing injection at your dentist, a direct descendant of the discovery called Coca-Cola made with a few drops of water. It is in the red can in your refrigerator. Flavored with legally imported, carefully stripped coca leaf. It is statistically speaking riding in trace amounts on the cash in your pocket. And high in the valleys of Bolivia tomorrow morning, a farmer will tuck a wad of green leaves into his cheek before climbing to his field. Exactly as his ancestors did before the pyramids were built. 8,000 years and the leaf has not changed at all. Everything around it did. Coca was never just a drug. [music] It never was. If this story surprised you, do me a favor and hit subscribe and tell me in the comments which chapter you did not see coming. The Popes, the surgeons, or the hippos.
